CHINA’S NUCLEAR BOMB IS NOT A MISSILE. 

IT IS TAIWAN: THE REAL GLOBAL RISK

Taiwan is not just a geopolitical flashpoint. It is the most dangerous single-point-of-failure in the modern global economy.

If China moves on Taiwan, markets will not see a routine geopolitical selloff. They will see a violent repricing of:

>> technology
>> trade
>> shipping
>> U.S. strategic credibility

WHY CHINA WANTS TAIWAN

This is not just about history. For Beijing, Taiwan is:

>> unfinished civil-war business
>> a First Island Chain military breakthrough
>> a test of American alliance credibility
>> leverage over the world’s most critical semiconductor chokepoint

That chokepoint is TSMC.

WHY TSMC MATTERS

TSMC is not just a successful foundry. It is the industrial base behind AI servers, smartphones, hyperscaler capex, defense electronics, and advanced networking.

Key numbers:

>> 2025 revenue: NT$3.81 trillion, up 31.6% YoY
>> 7nm and below: 74% of full-year wafer revenue
>> 4Q25 advanced nodes: 77% of wafer revenue
>> 3nm: 24% of 2025 wafer revenue
>> 5nm: 36% of 2025 wafer revenue
>> 4Q25 gross margin: 62.3%
>> 4Q25 operating margin: 54.0%

THE BIGGER SEMICONDUCTOR STORY

Taiwan is not just home to TSMC. It is the core of the global advanced-chip ecosystem.

Key numbers:
>> over 60% of global foundry revenue comes from Taiwan
>> over 90% of leading-edge chip manufacturing sits in Taiwan
>> 2025 Taiwan semiconductor industry revenue: about $198 billion
>> 2025 industry growth: +19.1% YoY

That is why Taiwan is not just a military target. It is a systems target.

WHAT HAPPENS TO MARKETS IF CHINA INVADES

This would not trade like another regional war. It would be faster, larger, and centered on technology.

System-level impact:
>> St. Louis Fed warns of flight-to-safety, trade disruption, banking stress, inflation pressure, and fiscal strain
>> Rhodium estimates over $2 trillion of global activity is exposed
>> blockade simulations suggest global GDP could fall about 5%

Likely first market reactions:

>> U.S. semis, AI infra, consumer electronics, autos, and network hardware sell off first
>> NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Marvell, server OEMs, and hyperscaler capex names face immediate multiple compression
>> Asia takes the first direct blow
>> Europe gets hit through autos, industrial machinery, and telecom equipment
>> Treasuries, gold, and the dollar likely rally first
>> oil, freight, and shipping insurance likely spike
>> Asian currencies likely come under pressure

THE MORE LIKELY FIRST PHASE: COERCION

China does not need beach landings to start market panic. A coercion-first scenario could be enough:

>> cyberattacks
>> maritime quarantine
>> air and naval encirclement
>> customs pressure
>> cable sabotage
>> port intimidation

The panic begins when chip output, shipping access, or U.S. response credibility starts looking uncertain.
WHAT CHINA HAS ALREADY POSITIONED

This is not yet an invasion ring. But it is a normalized pressure perimeter.

Recent Taiwan defense data shows:
>> daily naval presence around the island: roughly 7 to 11 PLAN ships
>> plus 1 to 3 official vessels
>> aircraft activity often ranges from low single digits to 12 to 16 sorties
>> March 18: 36 PLA aircraft, with 24 crossing the median line
>> March 25: 16 PLA aircraft, 10 PLAN ships, 2 official ships
>> March 27: 6 PLA aircraft, 10 PLAN ships, 2 official ships

Additional pressure asset:
>> over 200 converted J-6 attack drones reported near the Strait
>> these are cheap saturation tools meant to absorb expensive air-defense interceptors

WHAT TAIWAN IS DOING

Taiwan understands the direction of travel.

Current response:

>> considering about $40 billion of extra defense spending
>> new U.S. arms package of about $14 billion reportedly on track
>> after a record $11 billion package in December
>> 66 delayed F-16V fighters expected to begin arriving this year
>> total F-16 fleet eventually rises to 200+ with upgrades
>> But Taiwan cannot win a prestige contest. It has to win a denial contest.

That means:

>> more mobile anti-ship missiles
>> more drones and sea mines
>> hardened command nodes
>> dispersed logistics
>> undersea cable resilience
>> faster U.S. deliveries
>> deeper coordination with Japan and the Philippines

BOTTOM LINE
The real question is not: Will China invade Taiwan?

The real question is: How much coercion can Beijing apply before markets, insurers, shippers, chip buyers, and allied governments start behaving as if war has already begun?

Because when the world’s leading-edge semiconductor base sits just 100 miles from the Chinese coast, the damage does not begin at invasion. It begins at credible disruption.

Nagsagawa ng joint ocular inspection sina Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) General Manager Usec. Nicolas Torre III, North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) Corporation President and General Manager Luis Reñon, at Valenzuela City Mayor Wes Gatchalian sa Caingin River sa Brgy. Veinte Reales, Rubber Master Road, Karuhatan, Valenzuela City ngayong araw, bilang bahagi ng Oplan Kontra Baha. 

Layunin ng inspeksyon na suriin ang patuloy na paglilinis at dredging operations na isinasagawa ng NLEX Corporation upang mapabuti ang daloy ng tubig at mabawasan ang panganib ng pagbaha sa lugar.

Ayon kay Torre, patuloy na makikipagtulungan ang MMDA sa mga proyekto at programa ng Valenzuela City at NLEX kaugnay ng Oplan Kontra Baha, bilang bahagi ng pinaigting na flood mitigation efforts sa rehiyon.

Patuloy ang koordinasyon ng MMDA sa pagsasagawa ng declogging, desilting operations, at iba pang hakbang upang maalis ang mga basura sa mga daluyan ng tubig at maiwasan ang pagbaha, lalo sa panahon ng tag-ulan. Kabilang dito ang regular na paglilinis ng mga estero, ilog, at drainage systems upang mapanatili ang maayos na daloy ng tubig sa buong Metro Manila.

Hinihikayat din ng mga opisyal ang publiko na makiisa sa pagpapanatili ng kalinisan ng kapaligiran sa pamamagitan ng wastong pagtatapon ng basura at pag-iwas sa pagtatapon nito sa mga daluyan ng tubig.

#mmda #mmdaatyourservice

data.text:
Since I posted about carpooling a couple days back, I’ve received around 30 emails. Not comments. Emails. From people who took the time to sit down, find my address, and write. 

Developers who already have the build in their heads. Students who want to do it as a thesis project. Mothers from Alabang, Paranaque, Marikina, all asking how to get it started in their villages.

Different backgrounds. Different ages. Different problems. Same solution.

And every single one of them asked me the same thing at the end.
Is this actually legal? Will I be impounded for doing this?

I’ve already answered this through an interview on CNN I did with former LTFRB chairman, Martin Delgra. He told me on live television that if no money is being charged through the platform, the LTFRB has no jurisdiction and no intention of stepping in.

But a quote from a former chairman in an old interview isn’t policy. And 30 people ready to build something real deserve an official answer, not just my word for it.

So here we are. Publicly. On the record.
With fuel prices squeezing every family in this country, traffic getting worse, and public transport not getting better, there are people ready to build something that costs the government nothing. No budget. No infrastructure. No procurement process. Just permission for communities to help themselves move more efficiently.

This is the kind of moment that defines how history remembers a regulator. Not the rules they enforced, but the ones they had the wisdom to step back from.

All they need is one sentence.

Something like: We support community-based, non-commercial carpooling initiatives.

That’s it. And suddenly those 30 people become 300. Then 3,000. Villages across Metro Manila start building their own systems. Families save money. 

Congestion eases. And the LTFRB gets to be part of the story that made it happen.
That is a good look. A proper solution, gift wrapped for them. All they have to do is publicly endorse it.

Because the alternative doesn’t play as well. Silence reads as complicity. A shutdown reads as exactly what everyone already suspects. That the system protects markets more than it moves people.

So here is the graceful exit. Take it. One statement. One sentence. That’s all it takes.

If you’re in favor of this, share this or tag the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board - LTFRB in the comments so we can all finally know one way or the other: Will the LTFRB support non-profit, community based carpooling apps or not?
